The calculation requires the unstated pointwise limit $f(x)=0$ for $x<1$; fixing one such $\\varepsilon$, for example $1/2$, would then match the negation of uniform convergence.","depends_on":[],"scope":[],"goal_refs":["main"]},{"node_id":"n3","text":"We can also apply Theorem 21.6: the convergence is not uniform since $f$ is not continuous.","claim":"Offers a second argument based on a cited theorem that allegedly makes continuity of the limit necessary for uniform convergence. Its applicability cannot be checked because Theorem 21.6 is not stated, $f$ is undefined, and the discontinuity of $f$ is not established in the proof.","depends_on":[],"scope":[],"goal_refs":["main"]},{"node_id":"n4","text":"\\end{proof}","claim":"Ends the proof.","depends_on":[],"scope":[],"goal_refs":[]}],"ambiguities":["The symbol $f$ is not defined in the theorem or proof; it presumably denotes the pointwise limit, equal to $0$ on $[0,1)$ and $1$ at $1$.","The proof does not explicitly establish pointwise convergence to $f$, which is needed to exclude uniform convergence to any other function.","The statement of Theorem 21.6 is unavailable, so its hypotheses and applicability cannot be verified.","The metric $d$ is not explicitly defined, though it presumably denotes the usual metric on $\\mathbb{R}$."]}
